t: and all his acts stand. What he does within the scope of his agency has halakhic validity.

and the one who appoints an agent does not need kinyan. No kinyan sudar (symbolic acquisition) is needed to give force to the agency (although in many places it is customary to perform a kinyan for it, to announce that the appointment was made seriously - see Hilchot Mechirah 5:11-13).

and witnesses are needed only to reveal the matter if one of them denies, as with all other claims. Witnesses are not needed to give force to the agency, but only to reveal what they agreed between them in case one of the parties denies (see also Hilchot Mechirah 5:9, Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:4).
he did nothing. His acts have no validity.
and likewise if he erred in any amount. That he bought at a higher price or sold at a lower price than the market price, even slightly.
he may retract. The principal may retract from the agency, and the sale is void.
for he says to him, "I sent you to repair, not to distort". The agency is on the understanding that it benefit the principal and not harm and injure him.

and they did not say that overreaching in movable property is a sixth. In an ordinary sale, when there is a difference of a sixth ("shtut") between the item sold and its market price, the cheated party may demand the difference back, and if the difference is more than a sixth he may cancel the sale (Hilchot Mechirah 12:2-4).

and slaves, documents, and land have no overreaching. In an ordinary sale of these there is no overreaching at all, even if the price difference is more than a sixth of the going market price (ibid. 13:8).
but an agent who erred in all of them by any amount may retract. See also ibid. halakhah 9.

and acquired for him without guarantee. That the seller stipulated that he does not take responsibility to return the buyer's money if the land is taken from him because of a lien for a loan and the like (see Hilchot Mechirah 19:8). But if the seller did not stipulate this explicitly, the law is that the sale carries a guarantee even though it is not stated in the bill of sale (ibid. halakhah 3).
this has distorted. For an ordinary sale carries a guarantee, and the agent should not have agreed to the seller's condition.

and the agent takes it for himself etc.. The commentators found it difficult why the agent's acts stand in this case and the sale is not void as in the previous halakhah. Many explained that this refers to a case where the agent did not tell the seller explicitly that he is an agent, and therefore the sale stands and the agent bears responsibility (as below 2:4, Kesef Mishneh and others).

and he turns around and sells it to the sender with a guarantee, since he bought it with the sender's money. But if the agent bought it with his own money, he may keep the land for himself and has no obligation to the sender (Sema, Hoshen Mishpat 182:10).
Therefore. Because the agent's appointment rests on the principle that an agent is sent to improve matters, not to worsen them.
cannot retract. The seller cannot back out of the transaction.
and the sender must give him according to the condition. The sender must reimburse the agent for what he spent, since he stipulated with him that he sends him whether to improve or to worsen.
a beit se'ah. An area of fifty by fifty cubits.
and sold him a beit se'atayim. Double what he told him.

this one has added to his words. The sale of the half of the field that the agent sold according to the sender's words is valid, but the agent added something he had no authority to do, and as to what the agent added without the sender's authorization, the sale does not take effect.
this one has deviated from his words, and the buyer has not acquired. In this case it is considered as though he did everything on his own initiative, and the sale does not take effect at all.
and did not specify. To how many buyers he should sell it.
even if he sold it to a hundred, his sale stands. Since this is not a deviation from his words, as he spoke in general terms and did not specify.
he has against him only a complaint. The sender cannot sue the agent, but can only complain that he did not act as told (see also below 7:6).

if the price of what he bought dropped, it dropped for the agent, because he is one who deviates. If the goods he bought became cheaper, the agent must pay the sender the difference and bear the loss, since he sent him to improve and not to worsen.

and if their price rose, it rose for the owner of the money. If the goods became more expensive the profit goes to the sender, since he bought them with the sender's money (for a similar law in a partnership see below 5:2).
and they added. The sellers, and gave him a larger quantity than is proper to receive for this sum.

whatever the sellers added to him belongs to both of them. Because where the price is fixed and known, it is clear that the addition is a gift given to the agent, and since this benefit came to the agent by means of the sender's money, they share it.
and if the item has no fixed price, everything belongs to the owner of the money. Because for something whose price is not fixed, the addition is not a gift but part of the sale.
to bother. To occupy himself and take trouble with it.

the agent need not bother to give it to him before witnesses. For one who lends to his fellow orally, even if he lent in the presence of witnesses, the borrower need not repay in the presence of witnesses (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 11:1); the same applies to a deposit (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 9:2). Therefore the agent too need not pay in the presence of witnesses.

and if he paid him without witnesses, he must pay. The responsibility lies on the agent because he deviated from the sender's words; and if the creditor claims he did not receive his money and sues the sender, the agent must pay.
and likewise if the debt was by a bond. When the debt is by a bond, the law is that it must be repaid before witnesses (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 11:1).

whether he told him, give him the money and take the bond. Even though the sender did not tell the agent to take the bond before giving the money, from which it might be understood that he relies on the creditor, the agent is obligated to carry out his mission completely.
and he gave without witnesses and did not take the bond. But if he gave before witnesses, even if he did not take the bond, the responsibility does not lie on the agent.
must pay. If the creditor sues the sender, the agent is obligated to pay.
and all three of them are standing. They are present and make claims before one another.

the agent swears a heset oath that he gave. The agent swears to the creditor or the worker that he paid, and is released from the claim. A heset oath is an oath instituted by the Sages for one who is sued and denies everything; it is lighter than an ordinary oath since it is taken without holding a sacred object (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:3).

and the worker or creditor swears a heset oath. Although ordinarily one who swears in order to collect money must take a severe oath while holding a sacred object (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 16:5), in this case they instituted that a heset oath suffices (for the reason see Sefer ha-Terumot, gate 29, part 2, par. 3, in the name of Rabbi Yitzhak Migash and Rabbeinu Ephraim; Tosafot Rid, Kiddushin 43b).

because they have a stake in their testimony, since they are obligated to swear a heset oath. For if we do not follow their testimony they will have to swear, so they have an interest in testifying, and one who has a stake in testimony cannot be a witness in it (Hilchot Edut 15:1).
In what case does this apply. That the sender obligates the agent to take an oath.

for there is no one there who makes a definite claim against him that he did not carry out his mission. Since the sender does not know for certain that the agent did not carry out his mission but is merely in doubt, he cannot make him swear, because a heset oath is not taken on a claim of doubt (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:7).
and a creditor comes to sue the borrower. And the lender claims that he did not receive the loan money from the agents.
for there is no one here who makes a definite claim against him that he took. Since the agents are not before us to say that they carried out their mission.

but the borrower pronounces a general ban. By enactment of the Geonim, in certain cases where a person suspects another of making a false claim against him and cannot obligate him to take an oath, he may pronounce a general ban (curse) on whoever lies against him in that matter, without mentioning the suspect's name (see Hilchot Gezelah 4:7-8; Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:4).
wrote. A document written in his own handwriting.
and said to him. Wrote to him in the document.
the maneh that I have with you. That you owe me.
if he wished to send it. If Shimon agreed to send it through Levi (for Shimon may refuse to agree and claim that he wishes to repay his creditor directly, as below 3:5).
he is not liable for its safety. Since Reuven agreed to repayment through Levi, Shimon is discharged as soon as he gave Levi the maneh, even if the maneh ultimately did not reach Reuven.
whether it was a loan or a deposit. Whether Reuven lent Shimon a maneh or deposited it with him.
provided that he recognizes that it is his handwriting. That it be evident to Shimon from the writing that this is Reuven's handwriting.
I did not write and I did not send to you. And he also claims that Levi did not bring him the maneh that Shimon owed him, and the letter is not now in Shimon's possession.
the borrower swears a heset oath that a letter in his handwriting came to him. Since he claims he paid his debt, he is like one who denies everything, who swears a heset oath and is released.
signs and marks between them in particular. Agreed-upon signs between them that appear in the letters they send to each other.

Shimon is liable for it and pays Reuven. Since he has no proof that it is Reuven's handwriting, he is in the position of one who does not know whether he paid, who must pay without an oath on the lender's part (Kesef Mishneh; see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:9).

and there is one who ruled that Reuven should swear and then collect. Because perhaps he really did write to him and forgot that he wrote, so he swears so that he will be precise in his claim (Kesef Mishneh).
like the law of all who swear and collect. Who swear while holding a sacred object (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:2).
Levi, who came as Reuven's agent and took fifty. From Shimon, in payment of his debt to Reuven (see Responsa of the Rif, no. 4).

Reuven swears that he did not send him but took twenty... like the law of anyone who admits to part. The commentators found it difficult why Reuven is considered one who admits to part and is obligated to swear by Torah law, when he swears in order to collect money from the borrower, whereas one who admits to part swears in order to be released from the claim. Some explained that Reuven is considered one who admits to part relative to Levi's claim that he gave him fifty while Reuven admits only to twenty (Shakh 121:12; see Kesef Mishneh and Bach, who explained in other ways).

and Shimon pays from his own house if he owed Reuven. For example, if the loan was by a bond, in which case Shimon must pay Reuven the missing thirty to complete repayment of the debt, and he cannot be released by claiming that he paid everything to Levi. But if the loan was oral, Shimon can be released with this claim (see Gra 121:39).
as it is stated. Regarding separating the terumah of the tithe from the tithe.

so shall you also lift up. From the added word 'also' the Sages learned that not only can they separate it themselves, but their agent too can separate it for them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 1:1).
a member of the covenant. A designation for a Jew.
and the same applies to the whole Torah. See also Hilchot Ishut 3:17, Hilchot Terumot 4:1.
even a married woman. Although the woman is under her husband's authority, another man may appoint her as his agent.
even a slave and a maidservant. Although they are under their master's authority.

and they are subject to some of the commandments. A Canaanite slave is obligated in the commandments in which a woman is obligated, and his master must circumcise him, and therefore he is included in 'member of the covenant'.
for business dealings. Monetary matters, but not for things in which they have no standing, such as agency for divorces and betrothals (see Hilchot Ishut 3:17, Hilchot Gerushin 6:6).
with an issar. A small coin worth a quarter of a ma'ah.

and measured out an issar's worth of oil for him and gave him the issar. The shopkeeper gave the minor an issar's worth of oil, or, if he had no oil, gave him an issar of his own so that he could buy oil from another (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 5:9).
and he lost the oil and the issar. The minor son lost the oil or the issar.
the shopkeeper must pay. The loss of the oil or the issar falls on the shopkeeper and the father need not compensate him for his loss (Rabbi Yosef Kafih; Bach).

for he sent him only to inform him. The father sent the minor to ask the shopkeeper to send him oil with a person fit to be sent with it, and did not intend that the shopkeeper send it with the minor.
he is discharged and not liable for its safety. Since from the moment of handing it to the agent appointed by the creditor, he is not liable for its safety (as above 1:5).

in the hand of one who appears to him fit to carry this thing. The condition includes any agent who is suitable for the mission, but it does not include sending it by a deaf-mute, an imbecile or a minor (Mishneh la-Melekh).
or the agent denied it. The agent claims that he received nothing from the sender.

the sender is exempt. Although in the case where the agent denied it, the sender must swear a heset oath as above 1:7 (Kesef Mishneh, who notes there that perhaps even in the case of theft or loss the sender must swear).
even though he pulled. Pulled an object in order to acquire it for the sender.
or he caused it to be drawn. The buyer can pull an object belonging to the sender in order to acquire it.
and it turns out that he deviated from his sender's intention, the sale is void and he returns. As above 1:2.

and if he did not announce that he is an agent, the sale takes effect, and the law is between him and the one who sent him. Although the agent deviated from the sender's words, the agency stands, but the agent must repair what he distorted in his mission (as above 1:3; various explanations were given for the distinction between the cases, see Netivot ha-Mishpat 185:5, Mahaneh Ephraim, Hilchot Shluchin no. 2).

I bought it for Levi. On behalf of Levi. The reason he said he is buying for Levi is to conceal the purchase so that he not be considered wealthy, or because he fears that challengers will arise against the purchase, and against Levi, who is a powerful man, challengers will not arise (Meiri, Bava Kamma 102b).
pays what he lost. By the law of an agent who deviated from the sender's words (as above 1:5).

the broker swears a Torah oath because he admitted to part. Since the seller claims a hundred from him and he admits to fifty, and one who admits to part of a claim is obligated by Torah law to swear (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:1; see Kesef Mishneh and Shakh 185:6, who discussed exactly which case is meant).

and if he had already given him the fifty, he swears a heset oath. Because after he has given the money he no longer admits to part but denies the entire claim of the fifty. Therefore he is not obligated in the oath of one who admits to part but swears a heset oath, which is a rabbinic oath for one required to be released from his fellow's monetary claim who denies everything (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:3).

and if the buyer knew... he returns the object to its owner. By the law of an agent who announced at the time of the act that he is an agent: if he deviated from his sender's intention, the sale is void (above, halakhah 4).

and he pronounces a ban etc.. If the buyer suspects that the sender really did give the broker authority to sell for fifty, but regretted it and is now lying and colluding with the broker in order to get the object back, he may pronounce a ban to threaten the seller (on pronouncing a ban see above 1:8 and the explanation).

on whoever gave him authority to sell for fifty, or agreed to fifty and retracted after I bought. The ban includes the possibility that the seller gave the broker authority to sell for fifty and retracted, as well as the possibility that he did not tell the broker for what sum to sell, and after he sold for fifty he agreed to the sale, but afterwards retracted (Sema 185:10).
the broker. An intermediary who sells property for the owners for payment.
he is an agent. He has the law of an agent of the owners, because he is not a merchant who buys from one and sells to another; rather the merchandise remains the owners' and is never his.
if he deviated from the owners' intention. Deviated from what the owners instructed him.
for this price. For this sum.
the buyer returns. The buyer must return the object, because the sale is void due to the seller's lack of agreement to the sale.

for he did not set a price for him and say, sell for such and such. Since Reuven (the sender) did not fix a specific sum for the broker, and the broker announced that he is Reuven's agent, any deviation from Reuven's wishes can be grounds for voiding the sale.
must pay because he receives payment. Since he receives payment for the brokerage, he has the law of a paid guardian, who is liable for theft and loss (see Hilchot Sekhirut 1:2).
to send them to his father-in-law's house. To send as a gift for his betrothed, who is in her father's house.
and said to him, if they accept them from me, I will pay their price. He made the purchase conditional on their being willing to accept them from him at his father-in-law's house.

and if not, I will give you a small payment. He stipulated that if they do not wish to accept the vessels, he will pay the craftsman for the benefit of having had the favor of sending the gift (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 81a).

and they were lost by accident on the way there, he must pay. Because he has the status of a buyer as long as it has not become clear that they do not accept from him, and a buyer bears full responsibility for what he bought, since it is his.

and if they were lost by accident on the way back, he is exempt. Since it has already become clear that he does not wish to complete the purchase, and since he benefited from the possibility of taking the vessels to his father-in-law's house without committing to buy them, he has the law of a paid guardian, who is liable for theft and loss but exempt for accidents (Tosafot Rid, Nedarim 31b; see Meiri and Rosh there, who explained similarly).
took them in order to sell them to others and said to him etc.. He made the purchase conditional on his managing to sell them in a certain place or by a certain time.

and they were lost by accident, whether on the way there or on the way back, he must pay. Although he bought them only on condition that he sell them in a certain place or by a certain time, nevertheless his intention is to sell them if he finds a suitable buyer even on the way back, and therefore he has the law of a buyer until he returns the vessels (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 81a).

swears the oath of guardians. The agent has the law of a person with whom something was deposited without payment, who must swear that it was stolen or lost, and that he did not lay a hand on what the sender placed in his hand (see Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 4:1).
and if the accident occurred in a place where witnesses can be brought etc.. If witnesses are available, he is not released by an oath until he brings witnesses.
jars of wine. Wine jugs.
with money he had in his possession. Money of the sender that was in the agent's hand.
and bought for him, and they were found to be vinegar. The wine in the barrels turned sour, and the agent claims that it turned sour after the purchase and that he was not negligent in buying.
such a large quantity that turned sour is publicly known. With such a large quantity, it can be determined through witnesses whether it turned sour before the purchase or after.
and if he does not bring proof, he pays. Since he can bring proof, he cannot be released by an oath that he was not negligent.
a hidden matter. That is not open to view.
for whose proof is not readily available. The damage occurred in a place where it is not common for there to be witnesses who can testify to it.

and the same law applies to any claim that a partner makes similar to this. Even with partners, where the partnership was in the possession of one of them and he claims that a loss occurred that is not his responsibility, he must bring proof if it is a matter that is visible to all.
if proof can exist. If it is common for there to be witnesses who can testify to such a claim.
as will be explained. Hilchot Sekhirut 3:1.
one who had land in the hand of another. Another person used it as an owner.
or had movable property as a deposit. He deposited movables with another person.
and wished to make an agent to litigate with this person. To authorize someone to sue in his place the holder of the land or deposit.
he writes him a power of attorney. A document in which he appoints the agent as his authorized representative.

and must transfer ownership by his hand that he authorized him. To transfer to him the thing he is claiming. The transfer meant here is a kinyan halifin (acquisition by exchange) by which he transfers the land or movables to the agent so that he can claim them for him ('kinyan sudar', see Hilchot Mekhirah 5:5 and the explanation there; and see below, halakhah 7, that when it is money he must transfer it to him along with land).
and the like in these matters. Another statement that means he transfers to him the thing he claims on his behalf.
because he says to him. The defendant can say to the agent.

even though he wrote him thus, he is only an agent. Even though he wrote him to litigate, acquire and take out for himself, and made a kinyan on this, he does not intend to transfer the things to him absolutely or in partnership, and this transfer is only to enable the representative to litigate for him with the defendant.

transferred to this representative a third etc.. That he made a kinyan with the representative only for part of what he claims, and for the remainder gave him permission to claim without a power of attorney (see Tzur Te'udah).
one of the brothers who have not divided. Brothers who inherited their father and have not yet divided the inheritance, and who therefore have the law of partners.
does not need a power of attorney from his other partners. And if he litigated with the defendant, the judgment stands.
for they say to him, why did you not come to claim, you too. Since he did not come, presumably he agreed that his fellow would litigate with the defendant.
in another country. In another city.

therefore the defendant may delay etc.. Because if the partner comes and makes this claim the judgment would be annulled, the defendant may delay the first suit and tell the plaintiff to claim only his share in the partnership.

a husband in his wife's property needs a power of attorney. Property that a woman brings into her husband's household for which the husband did not take responsibility is called 'nikhsei melog' (usufruct property); the law is that the principal belongs to the wife and the husband receives the produce (see Hilchot Ishut 16:1-2, 22:7). When the husband wishes to claim for his wife in her usufruct property, he must get a power of attorney because the principal of the land belongs to the wife.
for if there is no land, he has no produce. Ownership of the produce depends on ownership of the land, and therefore the husband has a share in this claim.
and made an agent before witnesses to bring them to him. Without a power of attorney.
if he wished to give, he is discharged... for he is giving to his agent. As above 1:8, 2:3.

and if he did not wish to give, he does not give, for this is not his litigant until he comes with a power of attorney. The defendant is not obligated to give the claimed object to this agent, because as long as he has not received a power of attorney he is not authorized to litigate with the defendant.

and anyone who comes with a power of attorney etc.. One who comes with a power of attorney enters a dispute that does not concern him, and conducting a case through other people creates hatred and strife (Meiri, Shevuot 31a; and see Hilchot De'ot 5:13 that it is not fitting for a Torah scholar to come with a power of attorney).

One who claims from his fellow in court... and he denied it cannot write a power of attorney etc.. The plaintiff can authorize another to litigate for him only when the defendant has not yet denied; but if he denied, the power of attorney looks false, since he is transferring something that, until proven otherwise, is not his. This applies only to movables or money, but with land, since it cannot be stolen and it is known and publicized that this land belongs to the plaintiff, even if he denied it he can make a power of attorney over it and it is not as though he is lying (Yekar Tiferet; see below end of halakhah 7).
cannot authorize another over him to make him swear. He cannot appoint a representative to go and make the defendant swear for him.

for there is nothing there that he can transfer to him etc.. Because a claim of an oath is not something that can be transferred to a representative; only a monetary claim, which can be transferred, can be the subject of a power of attorney.

a transfer by his hand is of no use here, since a coin is not acquired by exchange. When one wishes to make a power of attorney regarding money, one cannot transfer it to the agent by kinyan halifin ('kinyan sudar', see above halakhah 1 and the explanation), since a coin is not acquired by this kinyan (Hilchot Mekhirah 6:1).
Rather, how does he do it. To transfer the coin to him.

he gives him any piece of land and transfers the money to him along with it. He transfers to him land of any size, and together with it transfers the money he wishes to authorize over. This kinyan is called 'kinyan agav' (acquisition along with land), and the money is acquired this way even if it is not lying on the land acquired (see Hilchot Mekhirah 3:8-9, 6:7).
because the loan was given to be spent. The loan money is intended for use and is not owned by the lender.

and a person cannot transfer to his fellow something that does not yet exist. And therefore he also cannot transfer to the representative the money he will collect in the future (for this rule see Hilchot Mekhirah 22:1).

and there is no way for a person to transfer a debt except either in the presence of the three. There is a way to transfer an oral debt, by the lender, the borrower and the buyer standing together, and the lender transfers the right to collect the debt to the buyer.

and it is a matter that has no reason, as we explained. Transferring a debt in the presence of all three is a kinyan the Sages instituted and said that it has no explanation and nothing else is learned from it (ibid. 6:8). Therefore the debt cannot be transferred for the purpose of a power of attorney on the basis of this law.

or by transferring the promissory note itself by writing and handing over, because it transfers the lien in it. When the debt is by a bond, it can be transferred through writing, in which the seller writes to the buyer (on the bond itself or on other paper) that he transfers to him the bond and the content that the bond represents, and in addition he must hand the bond over to the buyer (ibid. halakhah 10). This kinyan is rabbinic, since the debt is not a tangible thing to which acquisition applies by Torah law (see ibid. halakhah 12), and since this kinyan is not a complete one, it cannot be used to transfer for the purpose of a power of attorney (Even ha-Azel).

But the Geonim enacted that a power of attorney may be written even for a loan. Although there is no way to transfer the loan money to a representative, they enacted that it could be transferred along with land, and in this way it would be possible to write a power of attorney over the loan.
so that each person not take his fellow's money and go off to another country. And the enactment allows him to sue the borrower even in another country through a representative.
he transfers to him four cubits of his share in the Land of Israel. From the portion he is due to inherit in the division of the Land.
and these matters. The reliance on land he has in the Land of Israel.
for who says that he has a share in the Land of Israel. Perhaps he is of the descendants of converts or freed slaves, who have no share in the Land (Kesef Mishneh; see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 11:17).
and even if he is fit, it is not in his possession. Even if he is entitled to a share in the Land, he has not yet acquired it.

for we do not say of it, let the law pierce the mountain; it is only to intimidate the defendant. This power of attorney is not absolute and its purpose is only to intimidate the defendant, and therefore the defendant may refuse to litigate with the representative (this refers specifically to a power of attorney made on the basis of four cubits in the Land of Israel, per Kesef Mishneh; some explain that this sentence refers to the Geonic enactment as a whole, and the defendant may refuse to litigate with the representative in everything the Geonim enacted, per Responsa Maharashdam, Hoshen Mishpat 129; see Mishneh la-Melekh).

for one who comes with this weak power of attorney is no less than an agent appointed before witnesses. If the defendant wishes to give to this agent, he is released from the claim and is not liable for its safety (as above, halakhah 5).

whether by witnesses of a kinyan. When the borrower made a kinyan before witnesses that he owes the lender, the witnesses may write the lender a bond without the lender's consent (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 11:1), and so the law of such a loan is that of a loan by a bond.

because it is a denial of the lien on land. From the moment the bond was written or the witnesses' kinyan was made, the borrower's land is pledged for the loan, so this is like a denial regarding land, which is not considered a denial for the purpose of a power of attorney (see above halakhah 6 and the explanation).

but an oral lender who was denied, they did not enact that they write a power of attorney for it. The Geonim limited their enactment to a case where he has a hold on the borrower's property from which a power of attorney can be made, or where he does not appear to be lying; but where he has neither a hold on his property nor, having been denied, does he avoid appearing to lie, they did not enact it.

and wished to cancel the agency... he may cancel it. Since the transfer for the purpose of a power of attorney is not a complete transfer but only for conducting the claim for the principal, the principal may cancel the power of attorney from one and give it to another.
therefore if he stipulated with him. If the representative stipulated with the principal.
one who comes with a power of attorney who waived the claim to this defendant. A representative who waived the claim to the defendant without prior agreement with the principal.
or sold to him. Agreed to sell the claimed object to the defendant instead of receiving it back.
or waived the oath for him. If as a result of the litigation the defendant became liable to an oath and the representative waived it for him.
he has done nothing etc.. By the law of an agent who deviated from his sender's words (as above 1:2).
therefore if he stipulated with him etc.. Just as this condition is effective for an agent (ibid. halakhah 3).

and this, my power of attorney, shall be with you. The power of attorney document will be given to the defendant so that he has proof that he gave to the representative and will be released from the claim.
and if the depositor authorized another, he has lost on his own account. In the case where the first representative does not give it to him.

and Levi said, there were never any such dealings, but let Shimon swear and collect. In principle a defendant who denied must swear a heset oath on his claim, but he can reverse the oath onto the plaintiff, who swears and collects (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:6; this refers to where he denied after the power of attorney was written, but if he denied before the power of attorney was written, a power of attorney cannot be written, as above halakhah 6).
and likewise all matters that Levi leaves up to Shimon. That Levi makes claims that require Shimon's presence.

he litigates with Reuven and the money is held until Shimon comes and is asked. So that Levi will not make such a claim assuming that Shimon will not come all the way to be asked and he will be released from the claim, the money is taken from his hand so that he will compromise with the representative and Shimon will not need to come to litigate himself (Kesef Mishneh).
to ban whoever makes false claims etc.. To intimidate defendant Levi with the ban (see above 1:7 and the explanation).

so that litigants will refine their claims. That they be precise in their claims and refrain from false claims, and not cause the Divine Name to be taken in vain and a false report to be raised (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:11).
when partners wish to form a partnership. To be partners in trade profits.
by what means does each of them acquire his fellow's money in order to be partners in it. So that they cannot retract from then on.
and both of them lift the purse. And by lifting the purse both acquire the coins by the kinyan of lifting.
but if they wrote a document and witnesses testified. They had witnesses sign a document in which the agreement to the partnership was written.

even though they made a kinyan by hand that this one would bring a hundred and that one a hundred and they would be partners in them. That they made a kinyan halifin regarding coins of a certain sum that they would bring and be partners in (this kinyan is also called 'kinyan sudar' - see Hilchot Mekhirah 5:5 and the explanation there).
for a coin is not acquired by exchange. Ibid. 6:1; see also above 3:7.
therefore if they became partners in other movables... they became partners in them. In which kinyan halifin is effective.

and they became partners in them, they became partners in them. After they actually brought the goods they had committed to, they became partners in them by virtue of the kinyan halifin they made at the outset, and need not make an additional kinyan.

and likewise if they mixed their produce. Even if they did not lift the produce, since people customarily take care not to mix their produce with others', the mixing itself counts as a kinyan for the partnership and no additional kinyan is needed (Sema 176:8; Kesef Mishneh wrote that this refers specifically to where they lifted the produce after mixing them).
or rented a place in partnership. And it became their courtyard, and when they placed the movables, both acquired everything by the kinyan of courtyard (Hilchot Mekhirah 3:7).
by any of the ways in which a buyer acquires. Detailed in Hilchot Mekhirah chapters 1-6.
craftsmen who formed a partnership in their craft. That they would divide between them the profits from each one's work.
that whatever this one and that one take for his work. Any payment they receive.

there is no partnership here at all, for a person cannot transfer to his fellow something that has not yet come into the world. Since they are not partners in the raw materials, there is no tangible thing to which the kinyan applies, for the profits are something that does not exist now (see Hilchot Mekhirah 5:14 and the explanation).
if they bought the garments with their own money, sewed them and sold them. If the tailors themselves buy the cloth and make garments from it and sell them, and do not receive them from the customer.
and bought the warp and weft with their money, wove and sold. The weavers themselves buy the threads used to weave cloth and make cloth from them and sell it.
and became partners in the money with which they buy. By the means of acquisition mentioned above, halakhah 1.
it is divided in the middle. They divide it equally.
a maneh. A hundred dinars.
and all of them engaged in the money. But if only one engages with the partnership money, the law is different, as explained below in chapter 6.
and they lost or profited. Lost or gained.

the profit or loss is between them equally according to their number, not according to the money. The profit and loss are divided equally according to the number of partners and not according to the sum of money each contributed. However, the initial investment is divided among them according to the sum each contributed, and only the profit or loss is divided equally. For example, in the case discussed here, if they earned a hundred and fifty dinars and the total is seven hundred and fifty dinars, the first receives a hundred and fifty, the second two hundred and fifty, and the third three hundred and fifty. And if they lost a hundred and fifty, the first receives fifty, the second a hundred and fifty, and the third two hundred and fifty.

and even if they bought an ox for slaughter etc.. Even if they bought something together in order to divide it between them proportionally according to the sum each brought, and in the end decided to sell it, they have the law of all partners and divide the profit or loss equally.
when they traded with the money they became partners in. And it is no longer in their possession.
and they lost or profited because of the coin that the king or the people of the country changed. Who made a decision to change the value of the coins.
they divide the profit or loss according to the money. Proportionally to the sum each gave, because this is a change in the substance of what they partnered in and not in profit or loss.
In what case does this apply. In which case is the profit and loss divided equally.
in general terms. When they did not stipulate explicitly how to divide the profit and loss.
these divide according to what they stipulated. Even though the division of profit and loss is contrary to each partner's proportional share.
or until all the partnership money is exhausted. Whereupon the basis for the partnership is gone.
the principal. The basic money that existed at the start of the partnership.
the profit. The partnership's earnings.

and if the merchandise is not subject to the law of division. The law of division applies to land and other property when the size of the property is such that if divided, its original name remains on each of the parts. When the property's size is not subject to the law of division, the partners cannot be forced to divide it and it must be sold whole (see Hilchot Shekhenim 1:1 and halakhot 4-5 there).
or its division would cause a loss. For example a vessel that would be ruined if divided.
these sell it and divide the proceeds. Likewise, one of the partners may buy the other's share (ibid.).
if there was a known time for the sale of that merchandise. And they did not agree in advance when the partnership would end.

each of them may delay etc.. For presumably they became partners on the understanding that they would wait until the customary time for selling that merchandise (Arukh ha-Shulchan, Hoshen Mishpat 176:49), for example if they bought olive oil that is customarily sold from Shavuot onward (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 31b).
unless they stipulated between them. That they may take earlier.
if they had a debt owed by others. That others owe them, referring to a case where they did not set a time, or set one and the time arrived.
we will not divide until all the debt owed to us is collected. And all the money will be in our possession.
rather they divide. The money that is in their possession.
and when they are repaid. The debtors who owe them.
each takes his share. From what was repaid to them.
if they are not responsible for each other. If each one undertook to collect only his proportionate share in the debt, and is not responsible for collecting his fellow's share.
they divide. What is in their hands.

and why may he delay, since his fellow says to him etc.. What is in the partnership is pledged to the partnership's needs, including the debt, so he may demand that the debt be covered from the partnership profits and also demand that they continue to engage in it together (Yekar Tiferet and Kesef Mishneh).

let us divide, and you take money against the whole bond and do business with it for yourself etc.. Let us divide the partnership money between us, and you take additional money against the whole debt, so you can continue trading with the money and when the time comes you pay the debt.
perhaps we will lose, and two profit more than one. Therefore he may demand of him that they continue to engage together with all the money.
one who gives his fellow money etc.. Paid him to sell or buy merchandise for him.
or until he sat in the shop. Until he conducted business in the shop, and if there are things there with a known time for their sale, until the time arrives (Yekar Tiferet).
he may not change from the custom of the country regarding that merchandise. See also below 8:4.
and may not go to another place. To sell it.
and may not enter into partnership in it with others. May not add another person to the partnership money.
and may not engage in other merchandise. So that he not neglect the shared merchandise (see also below 7:7).
on credit. A sale where payment is deferred to a later date.
he is exempt. He does not bear responsibility for a loss or damage to the merchandise.

and all these matters need no kinyan, only words. Unlike the original forming of the partnership, in which a kinyan is required. The reason is that the agreement is a waiver of the change and its consequences, and a monetary right can be waived without a kinyan (Kesef Mishneh, based on Hilchot Mekhirah 5:11).
or sailed at sea or went to another place. In order to sell the merchandise.
that comes because of what he transgressed. That is caused by the change.
the profit is in the middle. They divide it equally.
according to what they stipulated between them regarding profit. If it was agreed that they would divide the profit and loss differently, they divide as agreed.
to buy wheat with it for merchandise, and he went and bought barley etc.. For a similar law regarding an agent who deviated see above 1:5.
and if they stipulated between them. To deviate from the custom of the country, for example if they stipulated at the outset that they could sell on credit or trade in other merchandise.

one who gives his fellow money, and he bought produce with it for half the profit. That the manager will buy merchandise with the money, sell it, and receive half of the profit (see below 6:1 that such a partnership is called 'iska', since one gives money and the other manages it).
took for himself. To buy with other money that is not the partnership's.
of the same kind. And we do not suspect that he bought it for himself with the funds of the venture (Yekar Tiferet; see Kesef Mishneh, who explained the halakhah differently).
and when he sells, he should not sell both together etc.. So that no suspicion arises that he took for himself profits that belong to the venture (Yekar Tiferet).

and may not take wheat for himself etc.. Lest when he comes to the market and sees wheat on which more can be earned, he buy it for himself and take barley for the partnership. Therefore the Sages forbade him to take a different kind for himself (Even ha-Azel).
so that the money of both be equal in a bundle. That they be treated equally as though they were a single bundle.
even though he accepted upon himself any accident or any loss that may come to them. Due to the change.
and I will be chasing after you in court to extract it from your hand. Meaning I will have to sue you in court to receive my share in the partnership.
to store the produce until a known time. To wait to sell it until the time when it is customary to sell it, in order to earn a lot.

they have overreaching against each other. If one of them brought produce worth less than his fellow's or than what was agreed, this is overreaching (the laws of which are detailed in Hilchot Mekhirah chapter 12).

these calculate. When they come to divide the partnership between them, they first calculate how much the produce was worth at the time they became partners and so will know how much each has in the principal and how much they gained or lost (and they divide between them as above 4:3).
that the tax collectors forgave them. The customs collectors waived for them part of the tax payment due on the shared merchandise.
they forgave for the middle. The amount forgiven is divided among all equally.
and if they said, we forgave because of so-and-so. That the forgiveness is because of only one of them.
what they forgave they forgave to him. And the others must pay the entire tax on their share.
and one of the partners rescued. Rescued part of the partnership from robbers.
he rescued for the middle. Since they are partners, presumably he rescued for all.
and if he said, I am rescuing for myself, he rescued for himself. And not for all, because he separated himself from the partnership (Hilchot Gezelah va-Avedah 12:10).
a thing known to two partners. That it is publicly known that it belongs to both in partnership.

even though it is in the possession of one of them, it does not leave the presumptive ownership of the second all the days of the partnership. Even if one of them holds it with him, it is held as belonging to both until the end of the partnership.

and he cannot claim etc.. Ordinarily one in whose possession an object is, is considered its holder, and if another wishes to take the object from him he must bring proof. But an object of partners is considered in the presumptive ownership of both even if it is actually in the possession of one of them, and he cannot claim that he bought or received it as a gift from the other (for a similar law regarding partnership in land see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 13:8).
one of the partners who came to divide without his fellow's knowledge. In a case where the time of the partnership ended or no time was set for it (above 4:4).
even if they are laymen. They need not be qualified to judge monetary cases.
trustworthy. Who will not tilt the appraisal in favor of one of the partners.
and expert in appraisal. They know how to estimate the value of the items.
money is as though already divided. Because its value is defined, it needs no appraisal in order to be divided.
and he may. He is permitted.
divide not in the presence of a court. But by himself.
when the money was all one coin and equal. Of the same type and the same quality.
some of them good and some bad. For example if some were damaged or not easily traded.
only in a court. Three trustworthy men expert in appraisal.
It is forbidden to be partners with an idol worshiper. To form a business partnership with him.
lest he become obligated to him for an oath. The gentile to the Jew.

and have him swear by his deity. The Jew would demand that the gentile swear by his idol, and this is forbidden from the verse 'and the name of other gods you shall not mention' (Exodus 23:13), that it is forbidden even to cause a gentile to mention the name of an idol (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 5:10).
and we already explained in its place that it is forbidden to trade in produce of the Sabbatical year. Hilchot Shemittah ve-Yovel 6:1.
nor in firstborn animals. Hilchot Bekhorot 5:9.
nor in carcasses and torn animals. Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 8:16.
nor in terumah. Hilchot Terumot 12:21.

nor in detestable creatures or crawling creatures. Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 8:16. The rule is that anything whose prohibition is from the Torah may not be traded in, and if its prohibition is rabbinic, it is permitted to trade in it (ibid. halakhah 18).

and it appears to me that if he lost, he lost for himself because he transgressed. Since there is a prohibition in dealing in this merchandise, it turns out that he changed by engaging in something not customary, and he has the law of one who violates the rules of partnership, who bears the losses but shares the profits with his partner (above 5:2; Sema 176:39).
or from those who manage. One who received money from his fellow to manage it (below 6:1).
even though they stipulated a fixed time. And that time has not yet arrived.
for the money has already passed to the heirs' possession. The deceased's share passed to his heirs immediately upon his death and they are not part of the partnership.
even though the money belongs to one of them, this is called a partnership. Because the joint engagement in the matter is what defines it as a partnership.
and if they lost or profited. The money, from its value.
it is in the middle. They divide the profit and loss equally.
and they may. They are permitted.
as we explained. Above 4:3.

the Sages enacted that anyone who gives money to his fellow to manage it etc.. They enacted this because this arrangement is convenient both for the owner of the money and for the manager, as each takes on half of the responsibility (see Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 104b).
half the money as a loan. And so the money he received becomes his, and he is obligated to give other money in its place.
even if it was lost by accident. For it is his money that was lost.

and if the half that is a deposit was lost or stolen, the manager need not pay. For he has the law of an unpaid guardian, who is liable only for negligence (Hilchot Sekhirut 1:2), because he receives no payment for guarding the deposit money but for managing his money (Kesef Mishneh; see Ra'avad).

and they come to the dust of interest. The manager engages with the half that is a deposit without receiving anything in return (since the profits on this portion go to the owner of the money). And it appears as though he does this in return for the half he received as a loan from the owner of the money (see also Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 5:9).
dust of interest. A term for interest forbidden by rabbinic law because the addition is not fixed in advance (ibid. 6:1).
if he wished the profit or loss to be equal in the middle. If the owner of the money wants them to share equally in profit or loss.

like an idle worker of that work from which he was idle. We estimate how much he normally receives for his work, and how much he would be willing to deduct from this pay in order to rest and be idle from his work, and this sum depends on the amount of effort and toil in his usual work (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 4:6).

and if he has any other business to engage in with this one's money. If he has his own business, and while engaged in his own he can also manage the money of the owner without being idle from his work.
even if he raises for him one dinar for all the days of the partnership, it suffices. It suffices to give him a dinar for all the management, and so there is no problem of interest.
and if they lost or profited, it shall be equal in the middle. If he sets payment for the manager as explained here, he may set the division of profit and loss equally between them.
and likewise if he said to him etc.. Another possibility is that the payment for the management be setting aside a certain percentage of the profits for the manager instead of a fixed wage.
all the profit will be yours, a third etc.. That he first takes a certain percentage of the profit and the rest they divide equally (Kesef Mishneh).
since he has another business. And is not idle from other work in order to manage the money he received.
and if this manager was his sharecropper. Who works his field for a share of the crop.
and he had another business. And is not idle from his work in order to manage his money.

for the sharecropper is bound to the owner of the field. They were lenient here because in addition to this being only dust of interest and a case where he has other business, he also pays the sharecropper wages in produce for his work throughout the sharecropping period, so he need not give him special payment for the management (Yekar Tiferet).

And the Sages further enacted... and they did not stipulate any condition between them. This enactment refers to a case where they did not define the manager's pay in advance in any of the ways above, in which case the Sages fixed how much he receives.
that the manager's pay for that half that is a deposit will be a third of the profit of the deposit. In addition to the profit from the half defined as a loan.
which is a sixth of the profit on all the money. A third of the deposit is a sixth ('shetut') of the entire profit.

and if they lost... and he has a sixth in his profit on that half that is a deposit. The owner of the money deducts for him from the loss on his half that is a loan the sixth of the profit as pay for managing the deposit, so that he is left with a loss of a third.
there is one who errs and says. Regarding what was said in the previous halakhah about a case where they did not define the pay in advance.
if there is profit the manager takes half, and if there is loss he loses a third. That the tilt in favor of the manager is only in the case of loss.

but it is not so unless they stipulated about this explicitly. But in general terms, when they did not stipulate, the manager takes a sixth as his pay in every case. Therefore if he profits he receives two thirds, and if he loses he pays a third, as explained in the previous halakhah.

and likewise if they stipulated that the manager lose half... this is permitted. For if it was defined in advance so that the arrangement tilts in favor of the manager in profit relative to loss, there is no problem of dust of interest.

and likewise if they stipulated etc.. That any division is permitted as long as it tilts in favor of the manager, since in this way the management is not for nothing and is not forbidden as dust of interest.
his labor. His toil with the half of the deposit.
and my teachers ruled that this condition is effective only if the manager had other business. Similar to what was mentioned above at the end of halakhah 2.
as we explained. At the beginning of the halakhah.

for this is a forbidden thing and a condition is not effective in it. In the opinion of Rambam's teachers, since this involves the prohibition of dust of interest, a condition is not effective in it, and therefore if the manager's pay is not a sixth of the profit it is forbidden.

and this does not seem right to me. The permission is not based on the condition itself; rather, defining a transaction in such a way that it is advantageous to the manager involves no dust of interest (and this is not like what was said above in halakhah 2, where the transaction itself is divided equally between them but the manager is given pay for his management, and since this pay is given to him only in case of profit, they also required that he have other business so that it not be forbidden as dust of interest - see Kesef Mishneh on halakhah 2 above).

and if they stipulated that he lose a quarter and when profiting takes half. A quarter corresponding to the lender's portion, and a third of the three quarters of the deposit portion, which is another quarter.

my teachers ruled etc.. Until here the discussion was of an iska that is as the Sages enacted, half loan and half deposit. This halakhah deals with an iska divided differently, in accordance with the division of profits between the parties. So when the manager takes three parts of the profit and the owner of the money a quarter, the portion of the venture that is in the nature of a loan is three parts, and the remaining quarter is in the nature of a deposit. However, to avoid the problem of dust of interest, the manager must receive pay for engaging with the deposit, and by the Sages' enactment this is a third of the profit or loss on the deposit portion (above 6:3). The dispute between Rambam and his teachers is how to calculate this third in the cases mentioned here, where the venture is not divided between the parties as half loan and half deposit.

the manager loses three quarters of the loss less a third of the quarter. Three quarters of the loss correspond to his share in the venture that is in the nature of a loan, and from this sum he deducts a third of the quarter of the deposit, which he receives for his toil. So in total he bears two thirds of the loss.
the owner of the money loses eight. Six dinars corresponding to the deposit, and two more, which is a third of the deposit, being the manager's pay.

if there is profit he takes as they stipulated, and if there is loss he loses that portion plus an additional third of it. Where the stipulation concerns the division between them in case of profit, there is no need to add pay for the management, and the pay is given only if they lose (and likewise, conversely, where the stipulation concerns the division of losses between them, the pay for the management is given only if they profit).
you learn by this measure. The conclusion from this method of calculation.

he has against it a third of what the owner of the money takes. He receives from the owner of the money a third corresponding to the deposit portion (which is three quarters, since the manager has only a quarter).
and it turns out that this offsets that. His share in the loss is offset by his pay, for the manager loses a quarter (corresponding to his share) and gains a quarter (a third of three quarters).
and likewise if they stipulated about the loss. How much he pays if he loses, without addressing profits, then in profit the third owed to him as pay for the management is added.
the manager bears the loss as they stipulated. He loses the entire loss in his share, since that is what they stipulated.
and you add a third of what the owner of the money takes. In case of profit he also takes a third of the profit corresponding to the deposit portion.
they stipulated that if there is a loss the manager will bear a quarter. The manager will bear a quarter of the loss.

and if they profited he takes half. That is, a quarter of the profit as they explicitly agreed, plus a third of the three quarters of profit corresponding to the deposit portion, and in total he takes half of the profit.
and although these things that they ruled are reasonable. There is logic in the pay given for managing the deposit depending on the size of the deposit.
if you go this way it turns out that the manager might lose and still receive pay. It is possible that there will be a loss and the manager will in fact profit from it.
for example, he stipulated with him that the manager take one seventh as pay. A seventh of the profit, so that one seventh is loan and six sevenths deposit.
and they lost. The venture lost money.
it turns out that the manager takes a seventh more than this loss. Instead of the manager losing, he actually receives a seventh of the amount of the loss, as explained next.
I owe you one dinar according to the stipulation. A seventh of the loss.
and you owe me two, which is a third of the deposit portion. Since the deposit is six sevenths, and a third of that is two dinars.
and if he had lost fourteen, the owner of the money would have to give him two dinars. It follows from this that the larger the losses, the more the manager gains.
like the words of the sick. Only madmen, sick in their minds, could make such an agreement (per Rabbi Yosef Shilat in Rambam Meduyak; see Hilchot De'ot 2:1).

but the true way and law seems to me etc.. In Rambam's view, in case of loss the form of payment for the management differs from the case of profit. When there is a loss, the payment the manager receives is not determined by the proportional share in the deposit (as he receives in case of profit), but by the manager's own share.
that whatever the manager would profit. The portion that they agreed the manager would receive of the profit.
if there is a loss he loses two thirds of the portion he would have profited. We deduct a third of that amount as pay for his management of the deposit, and so he loses two thirds of his share.
and likewise if they stipulated about the loss. They fixed the manager's share in the losses.
and they profited. In which case the law is that the manager receives a third as his pay.

he takes like that portion in which he would have lost, plus an additional third of his fellow's portion. In this case he receives his pay for managing the deposit, corresponding to a third of the deposit portion.
you find yourself saying by this measure. By this method of calculation.
this one pays a sixth. A sixth of the loss, which is a quarter minus a third of the quarter.

One who gives his fellow money in general terms... or they stipulated explicitly that the profit and loss be equal between them. And they did not define the manager's pay. The law is that the venture is defined as half loan and half deposit (above 6:2), and the manager's pay is that he receives two thirds of the profit and bears only a third if they lost (as detailed above 6:3).

there is one who ruled that the manager pays a third, as we explained, if part of the money was lost. Above 6:3; according to this opinion it makes no difference whether all the money or only part of it was lost, and the manager always pays only a third of the loss.

and it seems to me that he pays half, which is in the nature of a loan. In every case the owner of the money does not lose the sum defined as a loan (for the reason mentioned later in the halakhah). This has implications for the case where all or most of the money was lost, in which the manager must return to the owner of the money the half defined as a loan, even if it turns out that he bears more than a third of the loss.

and what the Sages said, he pays a third of the loss etc.. The rule that the manager pays only a third of the losses applies only where the loss does not cause the owner of the money to receive back less than half his money, that is, the half defined as a loan in the manager's hand.
Reuven gave Shimon a hundred and twenty. Of which sixty as a loan and sixty as a deposit.
and he traded and lost ninety. And thirty remained in the venture.
Shimon pays thirty. Which is a third of the loss.
and it turns out that Reuven takes sixty. For he took thirty from the manager and thirty remained in the venture, so the whole sum corresponding to the loan is in his hand.
we do not say that Shimon loses thirty-five. Which is a third of the one hundred and five that he lost.
for if you say so. That Shimon pays only thirty-five.
it turns out that Reuven takes fifty. The fifteen that remained from the venture and the thirty-five that the manager paid him.

and Reuven never takes less than sixty. For this is the sum of half the venture that is in the nature of a loan. Therefore in the case discussed here Shimon pays forty-five, so that together with the fifteen remaining from the venture Reuven will receive sixty.
Therefore. The following law, which appears in the Gemara (Bava Batra 70b; and see below, halakhah 5), shows the correctness of the conclusion above.

an iska bond that came out against orphans. A venture written in a bond, and during the term of the venture the manager died, and the owner of the money sued the orphans on the basis of the bond, and it is not known what happened to the venture and perhaps all of it was lost.
the holder of the bond swears. Like anyone who comes to collect from orphans (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 14:1).
and collects half, which is in the nature of a loan. But he does not collect the deposit half, because we do not collect from orphans a deposit whose fate is unknown.

although we always make claims on behalf of the heir. The court makes in their place any claim their father could have made, and so they are exempt from the deposit half because their father could have made a claim that would exempt him; and from the fact that he collects the half corresponding to the loan, it is proved that there is no way in which the manager could be exempt from paying in full the half that is in the nature of a loan.

and why do I say that we do not deduct for him here against his pay for managing the deposit. For the Sages fixed that the manager pays only a third of the loss, so that the management not be for nothing and forbidden as dust of interest (see above 6:2-3). So why, in the case where all or most of the money was lost, do we not deduct from the manager his pay for the management?

for he takes only the loan half. For he takes only half of what he gave, which is the loan portion. And since the owner of the money does not receive the deposit portion at all, there is no need to pay for the management of the deposit (see another explanation in Even ha-Azel).

and likewise if they stipulated that the manager take a quarter of the profit. Then only a quarter of the money is defined as a loan, and in case of loss he pays two thirds of the loss corresponding to his share, which is a sixth (as detailed above, end of chapter 6).
he pays the whole quarter that is in the nature of a loan. Which the owner of the money does not lose in any case.

but if a little of the money remains etc.. For example, if he received two hundred, of which fifty are in the nature of a loan, and he lost one hundred eighty and twenty remained, if he pays a sixth of the loss, that is thirty, together there will be fifty, the sum of the loan.
for the reason we already explained. At the beginning of this halakhah, that the owner of the money receives the loan sum in every case (Merkevet ha-Mishneh).
and he loses two thirds of it, and we calculate the profit that we profited at the end and he takes a third of it. According to what was detailed above 6:3.
rather he calculates at the end. He calculates the final result of the venture at the end.
and he does not have. The manager.
he gave him two hundred sheets for two hundred dinars in an iska. Two hundred sheets worth two hundred dinars, for him to trade in them and divide the profits.
he calculates for him on each bond separately. Each bond is considered a separate venture.

and the owner of the money lost on his own account. The owner of the money loses if the ventures are split, since the share of profit (two thirds) the manager takes in profit is greater than his share in losses (a third); rather he prefers that there be one venture and the losses be offset against the profits.
and wrote him one iska bond for two hundred dinars. And thereby combined the ventures.
for if he sold the hundred sheets for a hundred and thirty. And profited thirty.
and the hundred barrels for seventy. And lost thirty.
the owner of the money takes everything. Because the manager receives pay in relation to profit (see above 6:3), and here he did not profit.
and he did not profit anything. For the whole two hundred is considered principal without profit.
but if he had left them as two ventures as they were. If he had left each venture separate.
the manager would have profited in his share on the garments twenty. Two thirds of the thirty profit from the sale of the sheets.
and lost in his share on the barrels ten. A third of the thirty loss.
I will take the half that is in the nature of a loan for myself and trade with it. And all the profit and loss will be mine.
and I will leave the half that is in the nature of a deposit with the court. To serve as trustees on my behalf for the owner of the money.
even in the Great Court. The Sanhedrin in Jerusalem.
he has done nothing. For he cannot divide the partnership, and so the half he is engaged in is still the money of the joint venture (see also Hilchot Mekhirah 7:12).
rather the profit or loss is between them in those ways we explained. Above chapter 6: divided as they agreed between them, or by the Sages' enactment where there was no prior agreement.
the manager who gave a gift etc.. Without the permission of the owner of the venture.
must pay. See Piskim ve-Shittot.
we already explained. Above halakhah 1.
without an oath. Since it is clear that they are his (see Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 6:4).

and neither a creditor nor the wife takes anything from them etc.. If the manager owes money to another person or to his wife for her ketubah, they do not collect from the venture, but only from the manager's share of the profits.
for half the profit. In return for half the profits.
he has against him only a complaint. He cannot sue him for this but can only express his anger at him (see also above 1:5).
of any kind he wishes. Any merchandise that falls within the category of produce (Kesef Mishneh).
one who sets up his fellow in a shop. To sell for him.
if he was a craftsman. One who practices a certain craft.
he should not engage in his craft. While he is sitting in the shop.
because his eyes are not on the shop while he is engaged in his craft. And this could cause a loss.

and if he was his partner in the shop it is permitted. If the owner of the shop is with him in the shop he may engage in his craft, and the owner of the shop can sell while he is engaged in his craft (Lechem Mishneh).

and he may not buy and sell other things, and if he bought and sold, the profit is in the middle. He should not engage in other kinds of trade because it would impair his attention to the shop's business. And if he transgressed and traded, the profits are divided between them equally as though this trade were part of the partnership (see Piskim ve-Shittot).
to set hens upon them. For hatching.
and the profit shall be between them. They divide the profit between them as with an iska.

he must raise for him the pay for his labor and feed. His toil and his expenses for the animals' food, so that caring for the egg owner's share not be dust of interest (as above 6:2, and see also Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 5:9).
and likewise one who appraises calves and foals for the shepherd. He estimates their value so that afterwards they can know how much they improved with the shepherd.
to manage them. To tend them.
and the profit is in the middle. The profit from the improvement they divide between them equally.
until it is able to carry a load. To bear a burden (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 5:4).
and he cannot sell without his fellow's knowledge within this time. As above 4:4.
the one who fattens must fatten it. In order to slaughter it after it has fattened.
the fat tail. The fat of the tail.
permitted. For the problem of dust of interest is solved, since the manager receives payment for his toil.
if the one who fattens had other animals that he fattens together with this one that is appraised with him. With the animal given to him for fattening.

even if he raised for him only a small thing... it suffices. Since he does not toil especially for the owner of the money but incidentally to his own, there is no dust of interest in this, as above 6:2.
and if he was his sharecropper etc.. See there.
his law is like the law of an iska of money. Above 6:3.
one appraises a cow, a donkey and anything that is accustomed to do. Work, and there is immediate profit in it in addition to the future profit when it is sold.
and the profit shall be in the middle equally. And he need not give him pay in addition to half the profit.
he has one profit for himself in the work of the animal. And it is considered pay for his management, and there is no dust of interest in this.
for he rents it out. He can rent it out to others.

and one does not appraise a calf with its mother or a foal with its mother etc.. On the basis that the profit from the mother's work will be pay for tending both, since pay is needed for the toil and feed of the calf or foal.
one who appraises an animal. A grown one.
until when is he obligated to tend it. In a case where they did not agree in advance how long he would tend it.

his fellow may delay him, because they became partners in general terms. And this is the usual time for these animals, and so each of them can delay his fellow from dividing before the time (compare above 4:4).
fattened. Made fat.
therefore he may delay him until the end of the second year. For ewes (and for she-donkeys until the end of eighteen months).
the offspring is part of the profit in the middle. The offspring is considered part of the profit and so its value is divided between them.
and in a place where it is customary to raise the offspring. And not divide it after a short period (as explained immediately below), but rather it continues to be part of the venture.
they raise. According to what was explained above, halakhah 1.
and divide. Immediately after this period, equally between them.
he sets them before three. Three men who are expert in appraisal.
for he has half the offspring. Half the offspring is his anyway as part of the profit.

and because he engaged with half of his fellow's, he takes half of that half. By the law of one who manages his fellow's animal. However, there is no need to give him pay for the toil and feed for caring for the offspring, since he toils the same toil also for his share in the offspring, and there is no dust of interest in this (Rashi, Bava Metzia 69a).
and if he did not stipulate so before three, he has waived. His right to profit in the animal owner's portion.
and the offspring are between them equally as they are. They divide them half and half.
a place where it is customary to raise a porter's fee for the money of the venture. If it is customary to pay extra for the carrying that the manager does, or when one must pay a porter to do so.
they raise. They calculate and add this to the pay that the manager receives.

and all the pay that the manager takes for what he carries on his shoulder is included in the pay of the money. That the recipient takes the carrying fee at the end of the venture from the money, and the remainder they divide between them (Even ha-Azel).

and likewise if it is their custom to raise the animal's pay. If it is customary to give additional pay to a manager of animals because of the great effort in caring for them, greater than in caring for a venture in other merchandise.

a place where it is customary to count offspring as pay for his toil. If the custom is that the pay for tending the animal is not a division of all the profit in its body and a division of the offspring, but he takes the offspring.
and any manager or partner in general terms must not change from the custom of the country. Above 5:1.
and all the surplus over the expense will be between them. Shimon takes from the produce the amount he spends on the field, and the profit that remains they divide between them.

all this is permitted and there is no dust of interest here. Unlike an iska in movables or animals, where half of the venture's value is defined as a loan, in land the law is not so, and so there is no problem of dust of interest.
a sharecropper says etc.. If at the stage of dividing the profit there is a disagreement about how to divide it.
who brought down sharecroppers on his wife's property. Usufruct property, whose law is that the principal of the land belongs to the wife and the husband is entitled to its produce.
and divorced her. And the law is that the land returns to the wife.
if the husband was a sharecropper, since the husband withdrew, they withdrew. Since the husband was a sharecropper, they came down as his sub-sharecroppers and agreed not to receive more than he did.

and they have from the expense only the amount of the improvement, and with an oath. Like the husband. And just as if the husband spent expenses on the land and did not eat of the produce the amount of his expenses, the law is that he swears how much he spent and the wife must pay him the expenses he spent if they do not exceed the amount by which the land improved (Hilchot Ishut 23:9).

and if the husband is not a sharecropper, they came down with the consent of the land and are appraised as a sharecropper. The law of the sharecroppers is as the law of any sharecropper explained above, halakhah 5 (see also Hilchot Gezelah va-Avedah 10:12).
the brothers. The sons of the deceased who inherited their father.
the other heirs. The deceased's brothers or his father's brothers and the like.
as partners for every matter. And all the laws of partnership apply to them (see also Hilchot Nahalot 9:1).

who fell into the king's service, the profit is in the middle. Who spent from the partnership's funds and gave to the king's men and thereby succeeded in obtaining a monetary benefit from the king (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 9:4; for a similar law regarding brothers one of whom was appointed to a post, see Hilchot Nahalot 9:6, and see Hasdei David, Bava Batra 10:2, who discusses the relationship between the two halakhot).
he was healed from the middle. From the partnership's money.
and the sharecroppers. Workers who work the field for a share of the crop.

and the guardians. Guardians, appointed to care for orphans and their property. [Note: the vocalization of the word follows the Greek original. In Rambam's autograph Commentary on the Mishnah the word is vocalized in several forms: sometimes the first pe has a kubutz, sometimes a patach (and in some places the pe is unvocalized).]
and a woman who does business inside the house. Who trades with her husband's money.
or whom her husband set up as a shopkeeper. In his shop.
and a member of the household. Who deals with the householder's money.

each of these swears by rabbinic enactment. A rabbinic oath, which resembles a Torah oath in that it is taken while holding a sacred object, holding a Torah scroll (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:2, below halakhah 4).
on a claim of doubt. Even if there is no definite claim against them that they stole money.
lest he robbed his fellow in the business dealings. In the course of the business dealings.
lest he was not precise in the accounting between them. When the manager rendered an account to the owner of the money, he was not precise in the accounting.
they rule for themselves. They rule leniently for themselves based on their own reasoning.
for two silver, which are two silver ma'ot. Two coins of 'ma'ah' made of silver.
as will be explained. Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 3:1-2, where the amount of these coins is explained.
but if he suspected them of less than this. If his suspicion arose only regarding a sum smaller than two ma'ot.
they do not swear. See also there, halakhah 7.

for he does not know for certain what his father suspected him of. The heir does not know for certain what suspicion his father had about that manager, and therefore does not know whether this suspicion concerned a sum of at least two silver ma'ot.
and in this it is proper to rule. In this way.

for the heirs make the woman who became a guardian during her husband's life swear. A woman who managed her husband's property for him during his life swears to the orphans if her husband dies (see above halakhah 1 and below halakhah 4), even when the orphans have no defined suspicion regarding two silver but only a general concern.
he swears while holding a sacred object. See above halakhah 2 and the explanation.
