for we do not say 'migo' to exempt him from an oath, only to exempt him from money. A 'migo' argument is where a defendant could make a good claim by which he would be exempt from the monetary claim, and he makes a lesser claim. The law is that he is exempt from the monetary claim even with the lesser claim, because he could have made the better claim ('migo' is an Aramaic word meaning 'since'; for an example of a migo claim see Hilchot Zekhiyah u-Matanah 9:22-23). The rule is that a migo claim is effective to exempt the defendant from a monetary obligation, but does not exempt him from an oath to which he is obligated (for further examples see Hilchot Sekhirut 2:8, Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 13:3).
for he may make him swear on a claim of doubt. The householder can make him swear in a case where he suspects him.
a guardian appointed by the orphans' father. The orphans' father appointed a guardian over his sons' property before his death.

the orphans do not make him swear on a claim of doubt. Since the guardian receives no pay for his work, they exempted him from an oath on a claim of doubt so that he not refrain from being a guardian. But if the court appointed him he is obligated to swear, because he benefits from gaining a reputation as a trustworthy person, since the court appointed him (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 52b; see also Hilchot Nahalot 11:5).

and likewise the woman etc.. The woman is made to swear only if she did business with her husband's money during his life or after his burial, but if she did business only between death and burial she does not swear.
guardian. A female guardian, in charge of his property.
about this which she used. A thing she dealt with.
she shall not sell for burial. She shall not sell from his property in order to fund the burial.
and the dead will be left unburied. By their delaying to bury him.
with the other. In the other's hand.
without weight, count or measure. And they relied on one another.
both of them entered into doubt. Because both engaged in the partnership and did not always make an exact accounting with each other.
they divided. They ended the partnership.
he cannot go back and make them swear on a claim of doubt. But he can place a ban on this, as below halakhah 9.

but if he had a definite claim, he makes him swear on it. Silence at the time of the division is not considered an admission that he has no claim, and so his law is that of anyone who sues his fellow with a definite claim, who can make him swear a heset oath.

and he rolls into it whatever he wishes. He can include in the present oath that he makes the defendant swear all the claims he has in monetary matters, including the claims of doubt about the time when they were partners, and he swears on everything together (for the law of rolling an oath, see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:12).
rabbinic. An oath by rabbinic enactment.
and debts owed by others remained to them. Debts that others owe them from the time of the partnership that they did not divide because they have not yet collected them.
they cannot make one another swear on a doubt etc.. Since the partnership has ended, and the debt that remains to be divided is a clear matter about which there is nothing to suspect.
in a purse. In a purse that belongs to the partnership.
and they already knew them. Both know how much money is in the purse.
for money is as though already divided. See also above 5:9.

and likewise if they made a reckoning of the whole partnership etc.. They calculated the total amount of the partnership, and there remained in the hand of one of them something of known value that belongs to his partner.
even though they have not yet taken it, this is his share. The thing they did not take has the law of an ordinary debt or deposit.
and they have not yet divided them and did not know their weight. So they cannot be regarded as divided.
as we said. Above halakhah 7.
but he may place a general ban etc.. He may pronounce a ban in general language on whoever robbed him when he was his partner and the like and did not admit it (see above 1:7 and the explanation).
for such was the condition between us. That we made a certain condition in the partnership.
or claimed that my principal was such and such. And therefore this must be taken into account in the division.
or claimed that I already gave you from the partnership. And therefore this sum must be deducted at the time of division.
or claimed that this merchandise is mine. It was bought with my money.
and the other says it belongs to the middle. That it was bought with the partnership money.
in the hand of the plaintiff, with an oath. The plaintiff can choose in which manner to make him swear, as explained next.

if the plaintiff wished etc.. The plaintiff can choose whether to make him swear a heset oath on the claim he is now making against him, or to make him swear the partners' oath and roll the present claim into it. Each oath has an advantage: the partners' oath is a severe oath taken while holding a sacred object, holding a Torah scroll (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:2), whereas a heset oath is a light oath without holding an object (ibid. halakhah 3). On the other hand, the plaintiff may prefer to make him swear in a limited way on the present claim he has against him, and if he later suspects him, make him swear the partners' oath (per Arukh ha-Shulchan 93:13; see there that the heset oath has a further advantage in that he can reverse the oath).
that you did not rob me of anything all the days of the partnership. This is the partners' oath.
and that there was a condition between us etc.. These are the claims that he rolls onto him within the partners' oath, as above 9:7.
we already divided and nothing of yours remains with me. And after they divided without claims, one cannot go back and make him swear the partners' oath (above 9:7).
we divided on the condition that we may make you swear the partners' oath whenever we wish. Such was an explicit condition between us.
rejects. Pushes aside.
cannot make him swear on a claim of doubt. He cannot obligate him to the partners' oath on a doubt. But if he has a definite claim, he can make him swear a heset oath as above 9:7.
and something remains of yours with me. From the partnership money.
and this remainder is only a debt that you charged to me etc.. The defendant claims that what remained in his hand after the division was defined as a debt or a deposit.

he cannot make him swear on a claim of doubt. He cannot make him swear the partners' oath, from doubt, that he did not steal from the partnership money, since the partnership between them has ended and the debt or deposit is not considered part of the partnership (as above 9:8).

and he cannot make him swear a heset oath that they already divided or that they were never partners. When the defendant does not agree to swear the partners' oath, claiming that they already divided or that they were never partners, and the plaintiff demands that he swear on this very claim, he cannot make him swear a heset oath on this, not even by rolling, as explained next.
for we do not make one swear a heset oath. See also Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:15.
and we do not roll. Ibid. halakhah 13.

but a matter in which even if he admitted it he would be obligated only to an oath, he does not swear on it. In this case, even if the defendant admits that he had a partnership with the plaintiff, he would not be obligated to pay money but to swear the partners' oath, since the plaintiff does not make a definite claim against the defendant that he took money from him but only demands that he swear that he did not do so.
claimed that you are still my partner and such and such remains with you. And wants to make him swear the partners' oath while holding a sacred object.
the defendant swears a heset oath that he has nothing in his hand. Because he has a definite monetary claim, and it is like any claim that obligates the defendant to a heset oath.

and he rolls onto him that you never robbed me of anything. Since he makes him swear on his definite claim, he can roll onto him that he swear also on the doubt whether he robbed him during the time of the partnership.
and he does not roll onto him... for the reason we explained. Above halakhah 2, that even if he admits his claim he would not be obligated to pay but only to swear.

and the defendant afterward went back and said, we divided. He retracted and admitted that they were partners, but claimed that he is exempt from the oath because they already divided the partnership.

we do not listen to him, for he is presumed a liar regarding this oath, and he swears the partners' oath. His second claim, that they divided the partnership, is not accepted, because there are witnesses that he lied about the existence of the partnership between them. On the other hand, he is trusted to swear the partners' oath that he did not steal, since he was not presumed a liar regarding the money itself, for perhaps none of the partnership money remained with him (Sema 93:20).
and likewise anything similar to this. If there are witnesses that he lied, he is not believed to make an exempting claim in the same matter.
and they traded together. And although each gave a different amount, their law is that they divide profit or loss equally (as above 4:3).

and Reuven claimed that the entire principal lost five hundred. And only a hundred remained. Since they are supposed to share the losses, Reuven wants to take for himself the whole hundred, and in addition that Shimon give him fifty so that each loses two hundred fifty, and Shimon does not agree with him that the loss is five hundred dinars.

we do not say, let Reuven swear the partners' oath... and Shimon pay fifty from his house. For the reason explained below, that the Sages did not enact for partners that a partner swear on his claim and collect from his fellow.
rather Reuven swears the partners' oath. That he lost the sum he claims, and on the basis of his oath he will not have to pay Shimon.
and he keeps the maneh in his hand alone. Regarding the maneh in his hand he is believed, since he is in possession of it.
Reuven claimed that Shimon knows for certain of this loss we incurred. And if Shimon admitted this he would have to pay fifty from his house according to the calculation above.

he rolls onto Shimon. Since this is a claim involving a monetary claim, it can be rolled onto him within the partners' oath (as above halakhah 2). For Shimon too did business with their money, and he can be made to swear from doubt the partners' oath and further claims can be rolled into it (above 9:7).

and if Shimon did not engage in this partnership at all. And he cannot be made to swear the partners' oath (ibid. halakhah 6), he can be made to swear a heset oath like any claim whose admission would obligate to pay money.

and not only that etc.. Not only does Shimon not have to pay from his house if the above conditions are met, but he also need not pay from his share in the partnership money in his hand because of Reuven's oath.

if this was the maneh that remained in Shimon's hand. And Reuven claims that the rest of the partnership money was lost, and demands that Shimon give him the maneh in his hand as is due him according to his claim.

for a partner is not among those who swear and collect. The Sages enacted for certain kinds of plaintiffs that the defendant does not swear and is released, but rather the plaintiff swears and collects, but a partner is not one of them (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:2).

and be careful with this law, for rabbinic authorities already erred in it. They ruled that Reuven swears and takes the hundred and also that Shimon pays him another fifty from his house (Yekar Tiferet).

Shimon claimed that Levi has a debt against me in this partnership of a maneh. This is a different case, in which Shimon claims that he borrowed a maneh from Levi for the partnership, and therefore the debt should be repaid from the partnership, and Reuven does not agree with him.

if he had enough in his hand to cover the debt and could give it to Levi, he is believed. If Shimon has partnership money in his hand with which he can repay the debt, he is believed to give it to Levi (this refers to where the money is not known to be partnership money, in which case he is believed by a 'migo' claim, since he could have claimed that the money is his own - Yekar Tiferet, and as follows from the continuation).
and they pay the debt and afterward calculate. Reuven and Shimon calculate the division only on what remains.
or from the merchandise known to belong to the partnership. Even if it is in Shimon's hand, because he has no migo claim.

lest Shimon and Levi are colluding against Reuven's property. Perhaps Shimon and Levi planned together to extract money from Reuven by fraud and share it between them. And since Reuven is a partner in the money, it cannot be taken from him and brought to Levi, by the law of one who extracts from his fellow, who must bring proof.

and even if the loan was by a bond, Reuven need not pay anything from it. Even where Levi has a bond proving the existence of the debt, we still suspect collusion, for perhaps Shimon already repaid the debt and returned the bond to Levi so that he could sue on it a second time and extract money from Reuven (Yekar Tiferet).
but if Shimon claimed that Reuven knows for certain etc.. And therefore he must share in the payment.
Reuven swears a heset oath or by rolling. As explained above, end of halakhah 1.

and likewise if a bond came out against Levi in Shimon's name for a hundred dinars from partnership money. If there is a bond according to which Shimon lent Levi a hundred dinars of partnership money.

and Shimon said, I was repaid and returned it to the purse. Of the partnership, and according to his claim Levi is exempt. And the bond is still in their hands, and but for Shimon's claim Levi would be obligated, since the lender has a bond (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 11:1).

or Shimon said, I set him a time of a year or two. If Shimon claims that he agreed orally with Levi that he would repay in a year or two years, and but for his claim Levi would be obligated to pay after thirty days, like an ordinary debt (ibid. 13:5).

lest he is colluding against Reuven's property. Perhaps he arranged with Levi that he make a false claim in his favor and Reuven loses from the postponement of repayment, and so Shimon must bring proof of his words.
and how do we judge in this law. Whether Shimon claimed that Levi repaid the debt or claimed that its time was deferred.
and if Shimon did not bring proof. That Levi repaid the debt or that he set him a longer time for repaying the debt.
he pays from his house. Shimon pays from his own money to Reuven his proportionate share in the debt that Levi was relieved of paying.
and Levi is sued at the end of the time he said. Shimon sues Levi when the repayment date he claims he agreed arrives (and if he claimed that Levi repaid the debt, Shimon loses).
